# Epistemic limits of upfront research: what cannot be known before building, and how perfection-oriented orgs fold reality-contact into the upfront phase

Status: COMPLETE. Section order is 1.1, 1.2, 1.4, 1.5, then 1.3 (filled late), 1.6-1.9, then 2 (practice), 3 (conclusion table H1-H7), 4 (gaps).
Author: worker agent, 2026-09-30. Scope: external literature only; no repo claims.
Receipt convention: every claim cites a URL (+ page/section where a PDF was text-extracted locally with pypdf from the WebFetch-saved copy). "Paraphrase" is marked; everything in quotes is verbatim from the extracted text.

## 0. Bottom line (to be finalised)

Desk research (reading, reasoning, reviewing, planning) converges only on the *complicated* part of a problem: things whose cause-and-effect is knowable by analysis. Several hole classes are provably not closeable by more desk time, because the information does not exist until an artifact meets reality (Cynefin complex domain; emergent behaviour; human-intuition failure on rare interleavings; model-vs-reality gaps; user/requirement discovery). Perfection-oriented orgs do not reach near-zero post-baseline surprises by researching longer; they move *cheap reality-contact* (prototypes, executable specs, model checking, fault injection, iron-bird/hardware-in-the-loop rigs) INTO the upfront phase, and they declare the baseline only after those instruments stop producing findings.

## 1. Sources and what each establishes

### 1.1 Cynefin: complicated vs complex (Snowden and Boone, HBR, Nov 2007)
Source: D. J. Snowden and M. E. Boone, "A Leader's Framework for Decision Making", Harvard Business Review, Nov 2007. Text extracted from https://www.systemswisdom.com/sites/default/files/Snowdon-and-Boone-A-Leader's-Framework-for-Decision-Making_0.pdf (HBR landing: https://hbr.org/2007/11/a-leaders-framework-for-decision-making).
- Complicated = analysable by experts (PDF p.4): "Complicated contexts, unlike simple ones, may contain multiple right answers, and though there is a clear relationship between cause and effect, not everyone can see it. This is the realm of 'known unknowns.' ... those in a complicated context must sense, analyze, and respond."
- Complex = not analysable in advance (PDF p.6): "In a complicated context, at least one right answer exists. In a complex context, however, right answers can't be ferreted out. It's like the difference between, say, a Ferrari and the Brazilian rainforest." ... "This is the realm of 'unknown unknowns' ... In this domain, we can understand why things happen only in retrospect. Instructive patterns, however, can emerge if the leader conducts experiments that are safe to fail. ... They need to probe first, then sense, and then respond."
- The named failure mode (PDF p.6): "the temptation to fall back into traditional command-and-control management styles—to demand fail-safe business plans with defined outcomes." and "Leaders who try to impose order in a complex context will fail".
- Implication for the operator's loop: asking "are we 100% complete?" of a desk-research artifact is a sense-analyze-respond question. For the complex residue, the answer is "no" by construction, and more analysis only produces the next "one small other thing".

### 1.2 AWS use of TLA+ (Newcombe et al., 2014 tech report; CACM Apr 2015)
Source: C. Newcombe, T. Rath, F. Zhang, B. Munteanu, M. Brooker, M. Deardeuff, "Use of Formal Methods at Amazon Web Services", Amazon.com, 29 Sep 2014. Text extracted from https://6826.csail.mit.edu/2019/papers/formal-methods-amazon.pdf. Summary: https://blog.acolyer.org/2014/11/24/use-of-formal-methods-at-amazon-web-services/. (CACM version https://cacm.acm.org/research/how-amazon-web-services-uses-formal-methods/ returned 403 to WebFetch and curl.)
- Review is necessary but not sufficient (p.1): "We have found that the standard verification techniques in industry are necessary but not sufficient. We use deep design reviews, code reviews, static code analysis, stress testing, fault-injection testing, and many other techniques, but we still find that subtle bugs can hide in complex concurrent fault-tolerant systems. One reason for this problem is that human intuition is poor at estimating the true probability of supposedly 'extremely rare' combinations of events".
- Design bugs, not code bugs (acolyer excerpt): "the code faithfully implements the intended design, but the design fails to correctly handle a particular 'rare' scenario".
- Results table (p.3): S3 fault-tolerant network algorithm "Found 2 bugs. Found further bugs in proposed optimizations"; S3 background redistribution "Found 1 bug, and found a bug in the first proposed fix"; DynamoDB replication and group membership "Found 3 bugs, some requiring traces of 35 steps"; EBS volume management "Found 3 bugs"; internal lock manager "Failed to find a liveness bug as we did not check liveness".
- DynamoDB had been through everything else (p.7): fault-injection with a simulated network layer, long stress tests, "detailed informal proofs of correctness. Those proofs did indeed find several bugs in early versions of the design. However, we have also learned that conventional informal proofs can miss very subtle problems".
- Scale (p.3): "we have used TLA+ on 10 large complex real-world systems. In every case TLA+ has added significant value"; "7 teams"; engineers "learn TLA+ from scratch and get useful results in 2 to 3 weeks".
- Explicit limits (p.5, "What Formal Specification Is Not Good For"): two problem classes, "1) bugs and operator errors that cause a departure from the logical intent of the system, and 2) surprising 'sustained emergent performance degradation' of complex systems that inevitably contain feedback loops. We know how to use formal specification to find the first class of problems. However, problems in the second category can cripple a system even though no logic bug is involved." Example: GC pause -> client timeouts -> retries -> more load.
- Model-vs-reality caveat (p.11): "Formal methods deal with models of systems, not the systems themselves ... The designer must ensure that the model captures the significant aspects of the real system."
- Implication: two hole classes are distinguished by AWS itself: (a) rare-interleaving logic holes, not found by review/proof/testing but found exhaustively by a model checker (an upfront, pre-code activity); (b) emergent performance/feedback holes, not found by the model checker either; needs load/fault experiments on a running artifact.

### 1.4 Boehm spiral: risk-driven, not document-driven (IEEE Computer, May 1988)
Source: B. W. Boehm, "A Spiral Model of Software Development and Enhancement", IEEE Computer 21(5):61-72, May 1988. Text extracted from https://faculty.washington.edu/hazeline/misc/reserve/boehm_spiralmodel.pdf (OCR scan; page numbers are PDF pages).
- The operator's failure mode is named (p.3): "A primary source of difficulty with the waterfall model has been its emphasis on fully elaborated documents as completion criteria for early requirements and design phases. For some classes of software, such as compilers or secure operating systems, this is the most effective way to proceed. However, it does not work well for many classes of software, particularly interactive end-user applications. Document-driven standards have pushed many projects to write elaborate specifications of poorly understood user interfaces and decision-support functions, followed by the design and development of large quantities of unusable code."
- The stopping rule (p.9): "'How much is enough?' ... 'How much of requirements analysis, planning, configuration management, quality assurance, testing, formal verification, etc. should a project do?' Using the risk-driven approach, one can see that the answer is not the same for all projects and that the appropriate level of effort is determined by the level of risk incurred by not doing enough."
- Specs are allowed to be incomplete where that is cheaper (p.5): "risk-driven specifications ... can have varying degrees of completeness, formality, and granularity, depending on the relative risks of doing too little or too much specification."
- The risk-resolution toolkit is mostly reality contact, not reading (p.5): "This may involve prototyping, simulation, benchmarking, reference checking, administering user questionnaires, analytic modeling, or combinations of these and other risk-resolution techniques." and "If performance or user-interface risks strongly dominate ... the next step may be ... the development of a more detailed prototype to continue to resolve the major risk issues."
- Implication: Boehm's answer to "are we done researching?" is not "when the documents are complete" but "when the residual risk of not doing more is lower than the cost of doing more", and the instrument for the high-uncertainty risks (UI, performance) is a prototype, not a longer spec.

### 1.5 Toyota set-based concurrent engineering (Sobek, Ward, Liker, Sloan Management Review 40(2), 1999)
Source: https://sloanreview.mit.edu/article/toyotas-principles-of-setbased-concurrent-engineering (WebFetch of the public page; partial text). Citation details (SMR 40:31-40, 1999; three principles) from search-result snippets, not the full article: "(1) simultaneous mapping of the design space according to functional expertise, (2) 'integration by intersection' ..., and (3) establishment of feasibility before commitment" (paraphrase via search snippet; treat as secondary).
- The paradox (verbatim from SMR page): "Toyota considers a broader range of possible designs and delays certain decisions longer than other automotive companies do, yet has what may be the fastest and most efficient vehicle development cycles in the industry."
- Point-based failure (SMR page, paraphrase): conventional design "tends to quickly converge on a solution" and then modifies it; picking the wrong starting point yields rework.
- Implication: when a question cannot be answered by analysis, Toyota does not pick an answer and later discover "one more thing"; it carries a SET of alternatives forward, narrows them only as test data (prototypes, trade-off curves) eliminate members, and commits only once feasibility is shown. The upfront phase includes building and testing alternatives, and "feasibility before commitment" is the baseline criterion. This is the structural fix for "take-backs": a late discovery removes a set member instead of reopening a decision already made.

### 1.3 (filled) Reinertsen: information has economic value, and zero failure means zero information
Sources: D. G. Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow (Celeritas, 2009), book not fetched; primary quotes from Reinertsen's own author blog post "The Four Impostors: Success, Failure, Knowledge Creation, and Learning", https://www.goodreads.com/author_blog_posts/5042134-the-four-impostors-success-failure-knowledge-creation-and-learning (WebFetch extract). Book framing (175 principles, cost of delay as the key economic variable) from secondary summaries, e.g. https://productdevelopment101.substack.com/p/productivity-in-product-development-4bb.
- "In product development we create value by generating valuable information efficiently."
- "We create economic value when the benefit of the created information exceeds the cost of creating it."
- "Note that this graph maximizes at a 50 percent failure rate. This is the optimum failure rate for a binary test." and "minimizing failure rates drives us towards the point of zero information generation."
- "information is only worth the value it creates" (two technical paths with near-identical costs: do not spend test money choosing).
- Implication: (1) a research step whose outcome you can already predict (a desk re-read that will "confirm" the plan) generates almost no information, so repeated "are we 100% done?" desk passes have falling information yield but constant cost; (2) the high-yield steps are ones with roughly even odds of failing, which are typically experiments against reality; (3) the stop rule is economic: stop gathering a given piece of information when its expected value (the loss it would prevent times its probability) is below its cost plus cost of delay. "100.00/100.00" is not a stop rule in this framework, because the value of the last unknown is never compared with the cost of delay.

### 1.6 Brooks: plan to throw one away (The Mythical Man-Month, 1975, ch. 11)
Sources: chapter listing https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/mythical-man-month-the/0201835959/ch11.xhtml; quote and pilot-plant analogy via search snippets from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mythical_Man-Month and https://home.cs.colorado.edu/~kena/classes/3308/f06/lectures/31/index.html (secondary; the cs.virginia.edu PDF fetched was a 16-page excerpt without ch. 11).
- "Hence plan to throw one away; you will, anyhow." Brooks's analogy (paraphrase): chemical engineers do not move a process from test tube to 2,000,000 gallons/day in one step. They build an intermediate pilot plant to gain experience with scale.
- Implication: the first working system is itself an instrument of discovery. Brooks's claim is empirical: the pilot WILL happen. The only choice is whether it is planned and cheap (upfront) or unplanned and shipped (the operator's "one small other thing" after the baseline).

### 1.7 Spikes and tracer bullets
- XP spike (Don Wells, extremeprogramming.org, 1999; fetched over HTTP with curl, HTTP 200): "Create spike solutions to figure out answers to tough technical or design problems. A spike solution is a very simple program to explore potential solutions. ... Most spikes are not good enough to keep, so expect to throw it away. The goal is reducing the risk of a technical problem or increase the reliability of a user story's estimate. When a technical difficulty threatens to hold up the system's development put a pair of developers on the problem for a week or two". URL: http://www.extremeprogramming.org/rules/spike.html
- Tracer bullets (Hunt and Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer, 1999/2019; secondary via https://fullstackhub.substack.com/p/the-pragmatic-programmer-12-tracer): tracer code is "not disposable: you write it for keeps", a thin end-to-end slice; prototyping is "the reconnaissance and intelligence gathering that takes place before a single tracer bullet is fired", and its value "lies not in the code produced, but in the lessons learned."
- Implication: two distinct upfront instruments. A spike answers ONE named technical question (feasibility, performance, API behaviour) and is thrown away. A tracer bullet exposes the INTEGRATION holes (the seams between components, the deploy path, auth, data flow) that no component-level research can see. Both are cheap, time-boxed, and belong inside the research phase, not after the baseline.

### 1.8 Real options (reasoning; no primary source fetched in this run)
- Not independently sourced within budget. The shared logic appears in the sources above: Toyota's delayed commitment over a set of alternatives (1.5) and Reinertsen's economic value of information (1.3). Stated as reasoning, not as a citation: a deferred irreversible decision is an option; its value rises with uncertainty and falls with cost of delay. Irreversible, high-uncertainty decisions (data model, consistency model, external contracts) justify buying information before committing. Reversible decisions do not, and researching them to 100% buys an option you did not need.

### 1.9 Unknown unknowns ("unk-unks"): Loch, De Meyer, Pich, Managing the Unknown (Wiley, 2006)
Source: publisher/abstract pages, e.g. https://ink.library.smu.edu.sg/lkcsb_research/5479 and https://gov.wiley.com/WileyCDA/WileyTitle/productCd-0471693057.html (abstract-level only; book not read).
- Abstract (via search snippet): the book gives "causal explanations of why unforeseeable factors in novel projects make traditional project planning and project risk management insufficient", and proposes two responses: "Trial-and-Error Learning allows for redefining the plan and the project as the project unfolds; Selectionism pursues multiple, independent trials in order to pick the best one at the end."
- Implication: this is the project-management literature's formal statement of the operator's pain. Planning and risk registers only handle risks you can list. The responses to unk-unks are (a) structured learning loops that are expected to redefine the plan, and (b) parallel trials. Selectionism corresponds to Toyota's sets.

## 2. How perfection-oriented orgs reach near-zero post-baseline surprises

Common pattern across the sources: they do not remove reality contact from the pre-baseline phase. They make it cheap and exhaustive, and define "baseline" as the point where these instruments stop finding things.

### 2.1 Distributed systems at scale (AWS): executable specification + exhaustive model checking before code
- See 1.2. Model checking a precise, executable design spec (TLA+/PlusCal, 102-939 lines per system) found design bugs that had passed "deep design reviews, code reviews, static code analysis, stress testing, fault-injection testing" and "detailed informal proofs". One DynamoDB bug needed a 35-step trace. That depth is past the reach of human review, because "human intuition is poor at estimating the true probability of supposedly 'extremely rare' combinations of events".
- AWS also found a bug "in the first proposed fix" (S3 row, p.3). Fixes are designs too and need the same instrument.
- The limit AWS states: model checking does not find emergent performance or feedback collapse ("sustained emergent performance degradation"), and the model may not match the real system.

### 2.2 Aerospace (NASA): end-to-end, test-as-you-fly system testing
- Mars Polar Lander (1999), via search snippets citing the Mars Program Independent Assessment Team summary (https://sunnyday.mit.edu/accidents/mpiat_summary.pdf, redirected from cs.washington.edu; PDF not fetched within budget, so this is secondary): the most probable cause was spurious touchdown-sensor signals at leg deployment, which shut down the engines early. "During the test of the lander system, the sensors were incorrectly wired due to a design error. As a result, the spurious signals were not identified by the systems test, and the systems test was not repeated with properly wired touchdown sensors."
- NASA lessons-learned compilations (e.g. https://appel.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2013/04/725262main_49s_learned_from_nasa.pdf, via snippet) list "no end-to-end testing in flight configuration ('test-like-you-fly')" as a common mishap root cause.
- Implication: the hole class "the integrated system in its real configuration behaves differently from the sum of its verified parts" was not closeable by analysis or component tests. It is closed only by an end-to-end test in the real configuration, repeated after every configuration change.

### 2.3 Medical devices (FDA design controls): validation on production-equivalent units under use conditions is mandatory
- 21 CFR 820.30(g), text as displayed at https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/820.30 (note: FDA's QMSR, which incorporates ISO 13485:2016, replaced this section in 2026; the ecfr.gov fetch redirected to a bot-unblock page, so the current text was not verified): "Design validation shall be performed under defined operating conditions on initial production units, lots, or batches, or their equivalents." It must include testing "under actual or simulated use conditions" and "software validation and risk analysis, where appropriate." 820.30(f) is separate: "Design verification shall confirm that the design output meets the design input requirements."
- Implication: the regulator encodes the epistemic split. Verification (did we build it to spec?) can be done largely by analysis and test against documents. Validation (does the spec meet real user needs in real use?) must be done with a physical artifact in use conditions, because no document review can answer it.

### 2.4 Trading / HFT: the negative control
- Knight Capital, 1 Aug 2012, SEC press release 2013-222 (https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2013-222): the router "rapidly sent more than 4 million orders into the market when attempting to fill just 212 customer orders" in 45 minutes. Loss "more than $460 million". Cause: defective legacy code left in the router, plus new code "incorrectly deployed". SEC-identified gaps: controls "at a point immediately prior to its submission of orders to the market", "controls and procedures for code deployment and testing".
- Implication: this hole class (deployment-state and legacy-interaction faults: which servers run which code, which dormant paths a reused flag wakes up) lives in the operational environment. Design research cannot see it. It is closed by deployment verification, pre-trade kill switches and hard limits built in upfront, not by more design analysis. (HFT-firm positive-practice sources, e.g. simulation and replay harnesses, were not fetched within budget.)

### 2.5 Fault injection / chaos engineering
- Principles of Chaos Engineering (https://principlesofchaos.org/): "Chaos Engineering is the discipline of experimenting on a system in order to build confidence in the system's capability to withstand turbulent conditions in production." Rationale: "Even when all of the individual services in a distributed system are functioning properly, the interactions between those services can cause unpredictable outcomes." It advocates experiments on production traffic because "systems behave differently depending on environment and traffic patterns".
- Implication: the emergent-interaction class that AWS says TLA+ does not cover is addressed by experiments on the running system. Upfront, the analogue is fault injection and load experiments against the tracer-bullet system before the baseline.

## 3. Conclusion: hole classes that desk research provably cannot eliminate, and the upfront activity that eliminates each

"Provably" here means one of two things. Either the source states the information does not exist before interaction (Cynefin: cause and effect known "only in retrospect"), or a documented case shows that exhaustive desk-side methods (reviews, informal proofs) ran and still missed the hole (AWS, MPL, Knight).

| # | Hole class | Why desk research cannot close it (receipt) | Upfront activity that closes it | Stop signal for that activity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| H1 | Rare-interleaving / concurrency / failure-recovery design bugs | Deep design reviews, code review, informal proofs, stress and fault-injection tests all missed a DynamoDB data-loss bug with a 35-step trace; "human intuition is poor at estimating ... 'extremely rare' combinations" (Newcombe et al. 2014, p.1, p.3, p.7) | Executable spec + exhaustive model checking (TLA+/PlusCal + TLC) of the design AND of every proposed fix, before code | Model checker is clean on the stated invariants and liveness properties at chosen bounds. Note AWS missed a liveness bug because "we did not check liveness", so the property list is itself a checklist item |
| H2 | Emergent performance / feedback-loop collapse (retry storms, metastability) | AWS: formal spec is "not good for" "sustained emergent performance degradation", where "no logic bug is involved" (p.5); Chaos principles: correct services still interact unpredictably | Load and fault-injection experiments on a running tracer-bullet system (spike for the hot path; chaos-style experiments) | Measured behaviour under planned load/fault envelope meets SLOs with margin; no unexplained non-linearity |
| H3 | Model-vs-reality gap (the spec or plan describes a system that differs from the real one: environment, libraries, APIs, hardware) | "Formal methods deal with models of systems, not the systems themselves" (p.11); Brooks: pilot plant needed to learn scale behaviour | Spikes against the real dependencies (real API, real data volume, real OS/tooling); conformance checks between spec traces and implementation | Each load-bearing assumption in the plan has a spike or test receipt, not a doc citation |
| H4 | Integration / configuration holes (verified parts, broken whole) | MPL: systems test ran with mis-wired sensors and was not repeated; NASA: "no end-to-end testing in flight configuration" as a common root cause (secondary, 2.2) | Tracer bullet: thin end-to-end slice in production-like configuration, re-run after every configuration change ("test as you fly") | End-to-end slice passes in the real configuration; any configuration change triggers a re-run |
| H5 | Requirement / user-need validity (spec is internally correct but wrong for users) | Boehm: document-driven projects wrote "elaborate specifications of poorly understood user interfaces ... followed by ... large quantities of unusable code" (p.3); FDA separates verification (spec) from validation (use conditions), 820.30(f)/(g) | Throwaway prototypes put in front of real users / real use conditions (validation), before baselining the spec | Users complete the core tasks with the prototype; no new requirement category appears in the last N sessions |
| H6 | Complex-domain unknown unknowns (cause and effect visible only in retrospect) | Snowden and Boone: "right answers can't be ferreted out", "we can understand why things happen only in retrospect"; Loch et al.: unforeseeable uncertainty makes planning and risk management "insufficient" | Safe-to-fail probes and parallel trials (set-based / selectionism), with a declared plan-revision budget, not a plan-completeness claim | Probes stop changing the decision. Declared as residual risk with a revision budget, not as "100% complete" |
| H7 | Operational / deployment-state holes (dormant code paths, partial deploys, state of the fleet) | Knight Capital: legacy defect + incorrect deployment, $460M in 45 minutes; SEC cites deployment and pre-submission controls (2.4) | Upfront design of deployment verification, kill switches, hard limits; rehearsed deploys (dress rehearsal on a production-like fleet) | Rehearsed deploy and rollback succeed; guardrail trips in fault drills |

Desk-closable residue (for contrast): complicated-domain questions ("known unknowns": Snowden and Boone p.4) such as prior art, known failure modes of named components, regulatory text, and API documentation. Desk research converges on these, and here extra passes do have diminishing but real yield.

Methodological consequence for the operator's "no take-backs" goal (synthesis, not a citation):
1. Classify every open question as complicated (desk-closable) or H1-H7 (reality-contact-only) BEFORE spending more desk time. Boehm: effort is "determined by the level of risk incurred by not doing enough".
2. For H1-H7 items, the research phase must contain the instrument (model checker, spike, tracer bullet, prototype, load/fault experiment, deploy rehearsal). "100% complete" for those items means "the instrument ran and is clean", not "the document is complete". A desk pass cannot close them. Re-asking "are we done?" will keep producing "one small other thing" because each desk pass samples the same unclosable space.
3. Reinertsen's economics bounds the phase. Stop acquiring a piece of information when its expected value is below its cost plus cost of delay, and treat a predicted-to-pass desk re-check as near-zero information.
4. Carry irreducible H6 residue as declared, budgeted plan revisions (Toyota sets, Loch trial-and-error). This turns a "take-back" into a pre-planned narrowing step instead of a surprise.

- Not fetched within the ~30-call budget: Reinertsen's book text (blog used instead); real-options primary literature (1.8 is reasoning only); the MPIAT PDF (MPL finding via search snippet); positive-practice sources for HFT and for aerospace formal methods (e.g. DO-178C/DO-333, Airbus static analysis); the CACM 2015 version of the AWS paper (403). The "35 high-level steps" wording is from the CACM version via search snippet; the 2014 tech report table says "traces of 35 steps".
- 21 CFR 820.30 text is as displayed by Cornell LII. FDA's QMSR (ISO 13485 incorporation) supersedes it in 2026; whether the verification/validation split survives verbatim was not verified here. ISO 13485 clause 7.3.7 is believed to keep design validation, but this is unverified.
